analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate tax, eliminating taxes on the largest inherited fortunes.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 46 of 53 Senate Republicans cosponsoring, has sat in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or vote since February 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would eliminate the federal estate tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax, the two taxes on wealth passed down at death. It would replace today's unified estate-and-gift tax with a separate gift tax at a lower top rate of 35% and a $10 million lifetime exemption that grows with inflation. The changes would apply to deaths and gifts after the bill became law.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the very largest estates. The current estate tax only applies to estates above roughly $14 million per person (about $28 million for a married couple), and it exempts family farms and businesses from tax on most of their value, so only a few thousand of the nation's roughly three million estates each year pay anything. Full repeal would entirely free those largest inheritances from federal tax, and the new gift tax design would let wealthy families move money to heirs during life at a 35% top rate instead of today's 40%.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the estate tax entirely for anyone dying after enactment, so no inheritance of any size would owe federal estate tax.
Repeals the generation-skipping transfer tax, which today applies an extra tax when wealth skips a generation, such as grandparents leaving money directly to grandchildren.

Replaces the current system with a separate gift tax whose lifetime exemption is $10 million (indexed to inflation from 2010) and whose top rate is 35%, down from the current 40% top rate, letting the wealthiest families transfer assets to heirs during life at a lower rate.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. Whatever estate tax revenue disappears has to be made up by other taxpayers, by future spending cuts, or by more federal borrowing, so the cost is spread across everyone who pays taxes or depends on federal programs.

drawbacks.text: The repeal eliminates a tax that today falls exclusively on the very largest estates, so the revenue it raised would have to be replaced through other taxes, borrowing, or cuts — spreading the cost across the general public while the benefit stays concentrated at the top.

The bill retains a gift tax rather than abolishing wealth-transfer taxation entirely, so very large fortunes would still face a 35% tax on lifetime transfers above the exemption — a partial safeguard, though a weaker one than the current 40% rate.

The $10 million lifetime gift exemption is large enough that even multi-million-dollar gifts to heirs would go untaxed during life, opening more room for tax-free wealth transfer than current law allows in most years.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit goes almost entirely to a few thousand of the wealthiest families each year, while the lost revenue — tens of billions annually — would otherwise be paid by everyone through other taxes or borrowing. Supporters argue repeal protects family farms and businesses from being sold to pay tax, but current law already shields most of a family business's value and the first ~$28 million of a couple's estate, so very few farms ever face the tax. The tradeoff strongly favors concentrated wealth.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in February 2025 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Senator John Thune introduced the bill on February 13, 2025, with 46 Republican colleagues joining as original cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation, the same day.
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — appears in the bill's action history through the rest of 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nothing has changed: current law, with its ~$14 million-per-person estate tax exemption, remains in place, and no side has moved the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — the bill has gone nowhere

for.name: Sen. John Thune
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Death Tax Repeal Act of 2025 in the Senate.

for.name: 46 of 53 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors of the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 47 sponsors and cosponsors are Republicans — 46 of the 53-member Senate Republican caucus — and no Democrat or Independent has signed on.

industries.industry: Heirs of very large estates (estates above ~$14 million per person)
industries.note: Full repeal would permanently exempt the largest inheritances from federal tax, a benefit worth millions per estate to a few thousand families a year. The lost revenue falls on everyone else through other taxes, borrowing, or cuts.

industries.industry: Wealth management and estate planning services
industries.note: The bill's $10 million lifetime gift exemption and 35% top rate create new planning opportunities for high-net-worth clients, even as outright estate tax repeal would shrink the estate-tax-avoidance business. Either way, the industry's interest tracks the tax-minimization goals of the very wealthy rather than the general public.

industries.industry: Large family farms and closely held businesses
industries.note: Owners of large farms and family businesses would never face a federal estate tax. The gain is real but modest relative to the pitch, since current law already exempts most business and farm value and applies only above the ~$14 million-per-person threshold.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action nearly a year after introduction and no Democratic support, the bill is unlikely to move on its own — tax legislation generally needs 60 votes in the Senate to advance. Its realistic path would be getting folded into a broader tax package passed through the budget reconciliation process, which needs only a simple majority; whether its provisions survive such a package is uncertain.
